summary: Psalm 36 begins by describing the wicked person as self-deceived, deceitful, and committed to a way that is not good. It then turns sharply to praise Yahweh’s loving kindness, faithfulness, righteousness, judgments, protection, abundance, life, and light. The psalm closes with a prayer for continued protection and a final picture of the workers of iniquity fallen and unable to rise.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets human evil beside God’s expansive goodness without pretending the threat is small. Inside Book I of Psalms, it voices both moral discernment and trust in God as refuge.

context.author: The heading says, “By David, the servant of Yahweh,” but Psalms’ headings can signal authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much historical information each heading establishes.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public and private prayer.
context.date: Psalms is a collection formed over time; individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period, so one date for the whole book would mislead.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, where many David-associated prayers speak from distress, danger, trust, and praise. This poem itself moves from the inner life of the wicked to God’s steadfast care and the speaker’s plea for protection.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with compressed images, parallel lines, shifts of address, and a heading connected to performance: “For the Chief Musician.”

outline.heading: A heading for worship
outline.note: The psalm is introduced for the Chief Musician and associated with David, the servant of Yahweh, before naming a revelation about the wicked.

outline.heading: The wicked person described
outline.note: The speaker depicts self-flattery, deceitful speech, abandoned wisdom, plotting, and refusal to reject evil.

outline.heading: Yahweh’s vast goodness
outline.note: God’s loving kindness, faithfulness, righteousness, judgments, and preserving care are pictured on the scale of heavens, skies, mountains, and deep waters.

outline.heading: Refuge and abundance
outline.note: The children of men take refuge under God’s wings and are satisfied from God’s house, river, spring of life, and light.

outline.heading: Prayer and outcome
outline.note: The speaker asks God to continue loving kindness and righteousness, to keep pride and wickedness from driving him away, and then sees the workers of iniquity fallen.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. By David, the servant of Yahweh. A revelation is within my heart about the disobedience of the wicked: There is no fear of God before his eyes.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the heading and the first diagnosis of wickedness: life without fear of God.

keyVerses.text: Your loving kindness, Yahweh, is in the heavens. Your faithfulness reaches to the skies.
keyVerses.why: The psalm turns from human corruption to God’s goodness, using vertical images of height and reach.

keyVerses.text: How precious is your loving kindness, God! The children of men take refuge under the shadow of your wings.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s refuge image and makes God’s loving kindness the ground of safety.

keyVerses.text: For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.
keyVerses.why: The verse gives the poem’s richest image of dependence on God: life and light are found with God.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David and calls him “the servant of Yahweh.” Because Psalms’ headings can function in more than one way, readers differ on whether this line should be read as a direct author byline, a collection marker, or another kind of association. The poem’s speaking voice moves from observing the wicked to addressing God directly.

questions.question: What does the psalm mean by “the wicked”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “the wicked” is described by behavior and orientation: no fear of God, self-flattery, deceitful words, abandoned wisdom, plotting iniquity, and refusal to abhor evil. The word is not explained as a social class or ethnicity here; it names a moral pattern within the poem.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin so darkly and then suddenly praise God?
questions.answer: The contrast is part of the psalm’s movement. Verses 1-4 look closely at disobedience, while verses 5-9 expand the view to God’s loving kindness, faithfulness, righteousness, judgments, preservation, refuge, abundance, life, and light. The chapter does not deny evil; it places it beside a larger account of God’s character.

questions.question: Is “under the shadow of your wings” saying God has wings?
questions.answer: The verse uses an image for refuge: “The children of men take refuge under the shadow of your wings.” Psalms often speaks through images rather than flat description. The point in this chapter is shelter and protection, not a physical description of God.

questions.question: What is “the abundance of your house”?
questions.answer: The psalm says that those who take refuge in God “shall be abundantly satisfied with the abundance of your house.” It does not specify a building or ritual scene in detail in this chapter. The phrase works with the next image, “the river of your pleasures,” to picture generous provision from God.

questions.question: Does verse 6 say God preserves animals too?
questions.answer: Yes. The verse says, “Yahweh, you preserve man and animal.” In this chapter, God’s care is not limited to the human speaker; it is pictured broadly enough to include animal life.

questions.question: What does “In your light we will see light” mean?
questions.answer: The line is poetic and compact, so readers should avoid making it say more than the chapter says. In context, “light” stands beside “the spring of life” and belongs to the psalm’s praise of God as the source of life-giving good. Readers differ on how broadly to extend the image, but within the psalm it describes seeing or living by what comes from God.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask not to be driven away?
questions.answer: After praising God’s care, the speaker prays for that care to continue “to those who know you” and “to the upright in heart.” The danger named is “the foot of pride” and “the hand of the wicked.” The request is personal, but it grows directly out of the chapter’s earlier description of wickedness as an active threat.

questions.question: Is verse 12 a prediction, a prayer, or a vision?
questions.answer: The verse states the downfall of “the workers of iniquity” as if the speaker can point to it: “There the workers of iniquity are fallen.” Interpreters debate whether to treat this as confident vision, poetic certainty, or a prayer’s anticipated outcome. The chapter itself gives the result without explaining the timing or mechanism.

glossary.def: A repeated phrase in this chapter for God’s loyal, protective goodness; it appears in the praise of God and again in the prayer for God to continue it.
Wrongdoing or crookedness in the chapter’s moral language; it describes both the wicked person’s speech and plans and the workers who are finally fallen.
A place of shelter or protection. In this psalm, the children of men take refuge under the shadow of God’s wings.
An image in verse 9 for life found with God, paired with the line about seeing light in God’s light.
